newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Celuloza debut seen just above strike price.
newsitem.headline: Polish Celuloza debut seen just above strike price.

text.p: Poland's largest paper firm Celuloza SA Friday's should start bourse trade on Friday just above its public offering price of 20.5 zlotys, analysts said.

The state treasury sold 7.5 million shares or 15 percent of Celuloza on a special bourse session on Tuesday and the average allotment rate was 34.64 percent, but analysts said the demand was unlikely to result in a strong jump at the debut.

"There will surely be orders at 20.5 zlotys and it's hard to say if there will be higher ones as well, but if so I believe 25 zlotys is the absolute maximum," said Czeslaw Pospieszynski, an analyst at Bank Gdanski SA brokerage.

Analysts said the 20.5 zlotys, which made Celuloza's P/E at 13.5 was a fair value for the firm, saying the paper sector should be valued lower than the whole market's average 15.8 P/E, due to its high capital requirements.
But they said Celuloza offered better growth perspectives than other paper firms of the emerging markets trading at average P/E of 10, as it was less exposed to cyclical pressures.

Analysts said the possible growth on the debut could be limited after the firm showed only five-million-zloty net profit in the first quarter, which made its 73-million-zloty 1997 net forecast doubtful.
In 1996 Celuloza's net amounted to 73 million zlotys.

Analysts said the debut price on Friday would also depend on the whole market's trend, but it should not differ much from Tuesday's strike price as there were only a few days between allotting the shares and the bourse debut.
They said its large capitalisation of above $340 million could additionally attract foreign investors.

Analysts said Celuloza was a good long-term investment as it was likely to cut its costs and improve its earnings, due to better climate for paper firms expected in 1998 and expected benefiting from a foreign investor.

The treasury ministry earlier said it was negotiating the sale of a 65-percent stake of Celuloza to a consortium led by a subsidiary of South Africa's Mondi, a unit of Anglo-American Corp of South Africa, and expected to close the deal soon after the firm's bourse debut.
